arkeonix_features_subtitle: 12 critical modules already built and tested, so you can focus on your product.
arkeonix_feature_auth_desc: OAuth with GitHub and Google, passwordless magic links, JWT sessions in HttpOnly cookies. Edge-compatible and secure.
arkeonix_feature_rbac_desc: Role-based access control enforced in Edge middleware. Platform roles (USER, ADMIN) and org roles (MEMBER, ADMIN, OWNER).
arkeonix_feature_billing_desc: Checkout, customer portal, and idempotent webhooks. Three plans with server-side enforced limits. MRR calculated in the admin panel.
arkeonix_feature_teams_desc: Invite members by email, assign roles, revoke access. Pending invitation system with expiring tokens.
arkeonix_feature_apikeys_desc: Generate, revoke, and monitor API keys. SHA-256 hashing, never stored in plain text. Per-plan limits enforced.
arkeonix_feature_email_desc: 5 React Email templates: welcome, invitation, subscription created, canceled, and payment failed. Sent via Resend.
arkeonix_feature_admin_desc: KPI dashboard with Recharts charts and paginated audit log. Restricted to ADMIN and SUPER_ADMIN roles.
arkeonix_feature_i18n_desc: English and Spanish included with next-intl v4. Add new languages in 4 steps. Localized URLs.
arkeonix_feature_darkmode_desc: Detects system preference, persists across sessions. Toggle in the sidebar. Implemented with next-themes.
arkeonix_feature_cicd_desc: 5 GitHub Actions workflows (lint, test, E2E, build, deploy). Multi-stage Dockerfile for production. Docker Compose for local dev.
arkeonix_feature_ratelimit_desc: 4 Upstash Redis limiters: auth, API, strict mode, and webhooks. Per-IP or user-ID. Returns 429 with Retry-After.
arkeonix_feature_audit_desc: Immutable action log: actor, resource, organization, IP, and User-Agent. Compliance-ready. Fire-and-forget with Sentry fallback.

arkeonix_review1_text: I'd been trying to set up auth with Prisma and Next.js 15 for weeks. With this boilerplate I had it running in an afternoon. Multi-tenancy comes pre-built — something that would normally take me days.
arkeonix_review2_text: What surprised me most is that it's not a rigid template. It's your code from the first commit. No weird dependencies, no lock-in. Stripe and Resend integrated and working in minutes.
arkeonix_review3_text: For an agency that ships recurring projects, the Pro plan pays for itself on the first project. Having RBAC and audit logs already implemented saved us weeks of work.
arkeonix_author_title: Built by someone who uses it every day
arkeonix_author_bio1: I'm David, a QA Automation Engineer focused on infrastructure and DevOps tooling. By day I automate tests with Java and Selenium — but when I close my work laptop, I open it again to manage my private server with Docker, explore new dev tools, and ship personal projects from scratch.
arkeonix_author_bio2: I built this boilerplate as a foundation for my own SaaS ideas. After years of research I kept hitting the same wall: hours spent configuring auth, payments and permissions — things that should already be solved. So I solved them properly, once, and made it available to anyone who shares the same frustration.
arkeonix_arch_subtitle: Clean, modular structure ready for production from the first commit.
arkeonix_arch_desc: Each layer is separated by responsibility. No business logic mixed with UI, no scattered configuration across the codebase.
arkeonix_arch_item1_desc: Next.js App Router with nested layouts, auth middleware and per-tenant separation.
arkeonix_arch_item2_desc: Server Actions, Prisma queries and Zod validation. Client and server completely decoupled.
arkeonix_arch_item3_desc: Reusable components with shadcn/ui, Tailwind and variants defined in one place.
arkeonix_arch_item4_desc: Auth.js, Stripe, Resend and Prisma configured and ready to use from day 1.
arkeonix_arch_item5_desc: Schema with User, Organization, Membership, AuditLog and ApiKey. Migrations included.

rutas_description: Structured paths to learn development, QA automation, DevOps, and how to build tech products from scratch.
ruta_primer_empleo_tech_desc: From discovering what roles exist to sending your first strategic application.
ruta_primer_empleo_tech_section_roles_co:
The tech ecosystem has multiple specialties, and not all have the same entry barrier or salary. Frontend, backend, fullstack, QA automation, DevOps, data engineering, mobile... each requires a different technical foundation.

Don't choose by trend. Choose by what motivates you to solve problems: visual interfaces (frontend), business logic (backend), quality (QA), infrastructure (DevOps), or data (data). If you're unsure, try our role test to orient yourself before investing months in the wrong direction.
ruta_primer_empleo_tech_section_aprender:
You don't need to master everything. You need to master enough for a recruiter to see you can add value from day one.

Prioritize: one main language (JavaScript, Python, or Java), version control with Git, at least one modern framework, and the ability to deploy a real project. The rest is learned on the job. Don't get stuck in endless tutorials.
ruta_primer_empleo_tech_section_proyecto:
Your project should solve a real problem, even if small. A Netflix clone doesn't impress. A personal expense manager with authentication, database, and tests does.

Choose a problem you have or observe in your environment. Document the process: technical decisions, errors, solutions. That's what recruiters value, not the number of GitHub stars.
ruta_primer_empleo_tech_section_cv_conte:
Your CV has 6 seconds to convince. Remove everything irrelevant. Put your name, a professional email, LinkedIn, and GitHub at the top.

In experience, prioritize personal projects if you don't have work experience. Describe what problem you solved, what technologies you used, and what result you achieved. Use metrics: reduced loading time by 40%, automated X process. Don't list courses as experience.
ruta_primer_empleo_tech_section_linkedin:
LinkedIn is your storefront. Professional photo, headline that says what you do (not student of...), and an about section that tells your technical story in first person.

Post about what you learn. Don't wait to be an expert to share. A weekly post about a bug you solved or a new tool attracts more attention than an empty profile. Connect with recruiters and industry professionals genuinely.
ruta_primer_empleo_tech_section_aplicar_:
Don't send mass CVs. Customize each application. Read the job post, identify what they need, and demonstrate in your message that you have it.

Take advantage of internships at companies: many hire after the internship period. Prepare for technical interviews by solving real problems, not memorizing algorithms. And be persistent: the first application rarely works, but the tenth usually does.
ruta_primer_empleo_tech_section_errores_:
The worst mistake is waiting until you're ready. You'll never be ready. Apply with what you have and improve as you go.

Other mistakes: no portfolio, not updating LinkedIn, sending the same CV to every job, not following up after interviews, and getting discouraged after the first no. Every rejection is information: ask yourself what you can improve and apply it next time.
ruta_qa_automation_desc: Learn to automate testing with Java, Selenium, and best practices to enter the professional testing world.
ruta_qa_automation_section_intro_content:
A QA Automation doesn't just find bugs: they prevent them from reaching production. They design automated test suites that validate functionality, performance, and security of an application every time the code changes.

It's one of the roles with highest demand and lowest saturation. Companies need people who can build robust testing pipelines, not just execute manual test cases. If you like breaking things to improve them, this path is for you.
ruta_qa_automation_section_java_content:
Java is the most used language in enterprise testing. You need to handle classes, objects, inheritance, interfaces, collections, exceptions, and streams.

You don't need to be a Java architect, but you must write clean and maintainable code. Practice with logic exercises, read open source testing project code, and familiarize yourself with Maven or Gradle for dependency management.
ruta_qa_automation_section_selenium_cont:
Selenium WebDriver is the standard tool for automating browsers. Learn to locate elements (XPath, CSS selectors), interact with forms, handle popups and explicit waits.

Set up a Maven project with Selenium, TestNG, and a Chrome driver. Write your first test that opens a website, fills a form, and validates the result. That foundation will serve you for everything else.
ruta_qa_automation_section_cucumber_cont:
Cucumber allows writing tests in natural language with Gherkin (Given-When-Then). This brings testing closer to business and makes the suite readable by non-technical people.

Learn to define features, scenarios, and step definitions. Integrate Cucumber with Selenium and JUnit/TestNG. A project with well-structured Cucumber demonstrates that you understand testing from the user's perspective, not just the code's.
ruta_qa_automation_section_pom_content:
Page Object Model (POM) is the standard pattern for organizing UI tests. Each application page is represented as a class with its elements and actions.

This separates element location logic from the tests themselves, making the code maintainable. If a button changes, you modify one class, not fifty tests. Master POM before attempting more complex frameworks.
ruta_qa_automation_section_api_content:
APIs are the heart of modern applications. Learn to test REST endpoints with Postman, RestAssured, or similar tools.

Validate status codes, JSON structures, authentication, headers, and edge cases. An API testing suite is faster and more stable than a UI one, and companies value it enormously. Include it in your portfolio.
ruta_qa_automation_section_cicd_content:
A test that doesn't run automatically doesn't exist. Integrate your test suite into a CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins.

Configure tests to run on every pull request, fail the build on regressions, and generate visual reports. This demonstrates that you understand the software lifecycle, not just isolated automation.
ruta_qa_automation_section_practicas_con:
Independent tests, isolated test data, clear reports, screenshots on failure, and parallelizable suites.

Don't duplicate code between tests. Use fixtures or factories for data. Keep tests fast: if a suite takes more than 10 minutes, developers will ignore it. Document how to run tests locally and in CI.
ruta_qa_automation_section_proyecto_cont:
Your project should be a real testing suite against a public application or your own project.

Include UI tests with POM, API tests, a CI/CD pipeline that runs them, and a README explaining how to run it. That's more valuable than a hundred certificates. It demonstrates that you can deliver quality from start to finish.
ruta_java_selenium_desc: Master Selenium with Java: from your first script to a professional testing framework with CI/CD.
ruta_java_selenium_section_intro_content:
Java + Selenium is the most in-demand combination in enterprise testing. Java provides robustness and ecosystem; Selenium provides the ability to automate any browser.

This path takes you from your first script to a complete framework with Page Object Model, TestNG, reports, and CI/CD. It's not the shortest path, but it opens the most doors in the Spanish and European job market.
ruta_java_selenium_section_java_content:
Variables, data types, control structures, arrays, classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, exceptions, and file handling.

Practice with HackerRank or Exercism exercises focused on automation. You don't need to be an expert in Spring or microservices, but you must write clean, reusable, and well-structured code.
ruta_java_selenium_section_webdriver_con:
Set up WebDriver with ChromeDriver. Learn locators: id, name, class, tag, XPath, and CSS selectors. Handle forms, dropdowns, checkboxes, alerts, iframes, and multiple windows.

Implement explicit waits (WebDriverWait) instead of sleeps. Use ExpectedConditions to wait for visible, clickable, or text-specific elements. This eliminates test flakiness.
ruta_java_selenium_section_testng_conten:
TestNG is the enterprise testing standard for its power: parallelism, test dependencies, data providers, listeners, and integrated reports.

Set up a Maven project with TestNG + Selenium. Learn annotations (@Test, @BeforeMethod, @DataProvider). Use data providers to run the same test with multiple data sets. This drastically reduces code duplication.
ruta_java_selenium_section_frameworks_co:
Don't reinvent the wheel. Frameworks like Serenity BDD or Selenide encapsulate common patterns and provide professional reports effortlessly.

Start with Selenide for its simplified API and automatic wait handling. If the project grows, evaluate Serenity for detailed reports and living documentation. The important thing is that your framework is maintainable, not that you use the latest hype.
ruta_java_selenium_section_practicas_con:
Mandatory Page Object Model. Clear separation between page object layer, test layer, and utilities. Use of constants for locators and timeouts.

Externalized test data (properties, JSON, or test databases). Automatic screenshots on failure. Structured logging. Suites runnable both locally and in CI. A good framework is measured by how long you can leave it untouched and it keeps working.
ruta_java_selenium_section_cicd_content:
Set up GitHub Actions or GitLab CI to run your suite on every push. Use Docker to guarantee the same environment locally and in CI.

Configure headless mode to run Chrome without a graphical interface. Generate HTML and allure reports. Notify failures via email or Slack. A green pipeline that fails when there are bugs is the best business card you can have.
ruta_java_selenium_section_proyecto_cont:
Automate a real web application: it can be a public demo or your own project.

Include functional UI and API tests, organized Page Objects, TestNG with DataProviders, HTML reports, and CI/CD with GitHub Actions. Document everything in the README. That project is your best CV.
ruta_portfolio_junior_desc: Build a portfolio that proves you can add value from day one.
ruta_portfolio_junior_section_debe_conte:
A junior portfolio is not a project gallery: it's proof that you can build quality software. It needs at least one deployed and functional project, with clean code, tests, a professional README, and CI/CD.

It doesn't matter if the project is simple. What matters is that it's finished, documented, and demonstrable. A finished project is worth more than five half-done projects.
ruta_portfolio_junior_section_mvp_conten:
Choose a real problem and solve it with tools you already know. A task manager, an expense tracker, a simple clone of an app you use.

The goal isn't to impress with complexity, but to demonstrate that you understand the complete cycle: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. A well-done MVP is infinitely better than an ambitious unfinished project.
ruta_portfolio_junior_section_readme_con:
Your README is the first impression. Include: what the project does, why you built it, what technologies you used, how to run it locally, how to deploy it, and screenshots or GIFs of it working.

Write in English if you can, or at least include an English summary. Use build status, test coverage, and license badges. An empty or incomplete README conveys disinterest or lack of attention to detail.
ruta_portfolio_junior_section_deploy_con:
Your project must be live. Use Vercel, Netlify, Railway, Render, or any free platform. A repo without a demo is a book without a cover.

Set up a custom domain if you can. Make sure deployment is automatic: every push to main should update production. This demonstrates that you understand basic DevOps, not just development.
ruta_portfolio_junior_section_testing_co:
Unit tests at minimum. Integration tests if the project allows. A CI pipeline that runs tests on every commit.

Include test coverage in the README. Don't chase 100% coverage by testing meaningless lines. Cover critical cases and both happy and error paths. A project with tests conveys professionalism and care for quality.
ruta_portfolio_junior_section_cicd_conte:
GitHub Actions that lints, tests, and deploys automatically. This isn't optional: it's the difference between a junior who writes code and a junior who delivers software.

Set up at least two workflows: one for PRs (lint + test) and one for main (lint + test + deploy). Include badges in the README. This demonstrates that you understand the software lifecycle beyond writing code.
ruta_portfolio_junior_section_capturas_c:
Include screenshots of the project working. Even better: a GIF or short demo video. Recruiters won't clone your repo to see what it does.

Show the main interface, key flows, and error states. If it's an API, include request/response examples. Visual presentation reduces evaluation friction and increases the chances that your project gets seen.
ruta_portfolio_junior_section_errores_ti: Mistakes that make a junior look weak
ruta_portfolio_junior_section_errores_co:
Unfinished projects. Empty README. No deploy. No tests. Unformatted code. Commits with messages like fix or update. Outdated and vulnerable dependencies.

Each of these errors sends a negative signal: that you don't finish what you start, that you don't care about quality, or that you don't understand how teams work. Fix them before sending a single application.
ruta_ci_cd_basico_desc: Learn to automate the software lifecycle from the first commit to production.
ruta_ci_cd_basico_section_que_es_content:
CI (Continuous Integration) is integrating code changes frequently and verifying they don't break anything. CD (Continuous Deployment) is taking those changes to production automatically.

Together, these practices eliminate deployment fear, reduce production bugs, and accelerate value delivery time. In modern teams, deploying several times a day is normal thanks to CI/CD.
ruta_ci_cd_basico_section_github_actions:
GitHub Actions is the most accessible way to start with CI/CD. It's defined with YAML in .github/workflows. Each workflow has triggers (push, PR, cron), jobs (tasks), and steps (actions).

Set up your first workflow: code checkout, dependency installation, test execution, and build. Then add a deploy job to Vercel/Netlify/Railway. With that you already have a complete pipeline.
ruta_ci_cd_basico_section_pipelines_cont:
A well-designed pipeline has clear stages: build, test, security scan, deploy. Each stage depends on the previous one. If one fails, everything stops.

Use artifacts to pass data between jobs. Cache dependencies to speed up builds. Run independent jobs in parallel. Separate the PR pipeline (faster, no deploy) from the main pipeline (complete, with production deploy).
ruta_ci_cd_basico_section_testing_conten:
Tests in CI must be fast, deterministic, and isolated. If a test fails intermittently, developers will ignore it.

Configure parallel test runners. Use in-memory databases for integration tests. Generate coverage reports. Fail the build if coverage drops below a threshold. A pipeline that protects quality is more valuable than one that just deploys.
ruta_ci_cd_basico_section_deploy_content:
Deployment should be a button, not a ritual. Automate staging deployment on every PR and production deployment on every main merge.

Use blue-green deployment or feature flags to reduce risk. Configure automatic rollback if error metrics rise. Document the deployment process so any team member can do it (or better: so no one ever needs to do it manually).
ruta_ci_cd_basico_section_monitoring_con:
Deploying without monitoring is flying without an altimeter. Set up alerts for errors, latency, and service outages.

Use tools like Sentry for errors, UptimeRobot for availability, and your hosting platform dashboards for basic metrics. A good CI/CD pipeline includes a post-deploy verification stage: if metrics worsen, automatically roll back.
ruta_crear_saas_desc: From idea to first customer: how to build a functional and monetizable SaaS product.
ruta_crear_saas_section_idea_content:
Don't start with the idea. Start with the problem. Talk to 10 people who have that problem. If 8 would pay for a solution, you have a validated idea.

Don't build for months without validating. Create a landing page with a waitlist form. If no one signs up, pivot or abandon. It's better to know before investing hundreds of hours. The market doesn't lie.
ruta_crear_saas_section_stack_content:
Choose technologies you know well that let you move fast. Don't choose the trendy stack if you don't master it.

A typical stack for juniors: React/Vue + Node.js/Next.js + PostgreSQL + Stripe + Vercel/Railway. It's enough for an MVP and scalable to thousands of users. The important thing is that you can build and deploy alone, without depending on others.
ruta_crear_saas_section_mvp_content:
The MVP must solve the main problem with the minimum possible functionality. If the problem is managing expenses, the MVP is adding an expense and seeing a total. Nothing more.

Every extra feature delays launch and dilutes feedback. Launch in 2-4 weeks. It's better to have an ugly product that works than a beautiful one that doesn't exist.
ruta_crear_saas_section_auth_content:
Don't build authentication from scratch. Use Supabase Auth, Clerk, Auth0, or NextAuth. They're secure, battle-tested, and save you months of work.

For payments, Stripe is the standard. Set up Checkout Sessions for subscriptions or one-time payments. You don't need a complex billing system at first. A payment button and a users table is enough.
ruta_crear_saas_section_deploy_content:
Deploy from day one. Every commit on main should be in production. Use Vercel for frontend, Railway/Render for backend, and Supabase for database.

Set up your own domain from the start. Users don't trust free platform subdomains. A custom domain costs 10€ per year and multiplies the perception of professionalism.
ruta_crear_saas_section_marketing_conten:
Build in public: share your progress on Twitter/X, LinkedIn, and relevant forums. Every post is an opportunity to be discovered.

Don't wait until the product is perfect to start talking about it. Your first customers come from the community, not ads. Be transparent about what you're building, the problems you solve, and the numbers you have. Authenticity sells more than corporate marketing.
